title: Grade 4 French — Wed, May 20
description: Les articles — Day 3 of 5: Definite vs indefinite — when to use each
subject: french

questions.question: When do you use the DEFINITE article (le/la/les)?
options: When you mention something for the first time
When referring to a specific, known thing or a general category
questions.explanation: Le/la/les = THE. Use for specific things ('The dog I told you about') OR general categories ('Dogs are loyal.').

questions.question: When do you use the INDEFINITE article (un/une/des)?
options: When referring to a specific known noun
When introducing a non-specific person or thing for the first time
questions.explanation: Un/une/des = A/AN/SOME. Use when introducing a non-specific item: 'I have a cat' (any cat, not specific).

questions.question: Choose: 'J'ai ___ chien. ___ chien s'appelle Max.' (introducing then referring back)
questions.explanation: 'J'ai un chien.' (I have a dog — first mention, any dog). 'Le chien s'appelle Max.' (The dog is called Max — now specific, known).

questions.question: 'J'aime ___ chocolat.' (I like chocolate — general liking)
questions.explanation: 'J'aime le chocolat.' = I like chocolate (in general). General likes/dislikes use the definite article in French!

questions.question: 'Je veux ___ gâteau.' (I want a cake — any cake)
questions.explanation: 'Je veux un gâteau.' = I want a cake (any cake, not specific). Un → indefinite.

questions.question: Translate: 'Dogs are loyal animals.' (general truth)
options: Un chien est un animal loyal.
Les chiens sont des animaux loyaux.
questions.explanation: 'Les chiens sont des animaux loyaux.' General truth about ALL dogs → les. Animals (plural, non-specific in predicate) → des.

questions.question: Which is correct for 'I see THE cat'?
questions.explanation: 'Je vois le chat.' = I see THE (specific) cat. Le for masculine definite.

questions.question: Which is correct for 'I see A cat'?
questions.explanation: 'Je vois un chat.' = I see A cat (non-specific). Un for masculine indefinite.

questions.question: Fill in: 'Il aime ___ football.' (he likes football — general passion)
questions.explanation: 'Il aime le football.' = He likes football. Sports with aimer use definite article (le/la).

questions.question: After NEGATION (ne...pas), un/une/des change to:
questions.explanation: After negation: Je mange un gâteau → Je ne mange pas de gâteau. Un/une/des → de/d'.

questions.question: Translate: 'I don't have a car.' (after negation rule)
questions.explanation: 'Je n'ai pas de voiture.' After ne...pas, une → de. Je n'ai pas DE (not une).

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence: (I like music / general)
questions.explanation: 'J'aime la musique.' = I like music (general). Definite article for general tastes and likes.

questions.question: Why does French say 'J'aime le café' (with le) but English says 'I like coffee' (no article)?
options: French uses definite article for general likes; English doesn't
questions.explanation: A key French grammar rule: general tastes/preferences use definite article (le/la/les). English uses no article for generics.

questions.question: Fill in: 'C'est ___ beau livre.' (That's a beautiful book)
questions.explanation: 'C'est un beau livre.' = That's a beautiful book. Livre (masc, singular, non-specific) → un.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched (article → use)?
questions.explanation: Le/la/les = definite (specific, known, or general category). Un/une/des = indefinite (non-specific, first mention).
